planting.note: Transplant small divisions or rooted stem sections in spring into moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; self-rooting trailing stems knit together into a mat within a couple of seasons.

directions: This East Asian counterpart to the familiar North American partridgeberry forms the same kind of tight, evergreen, trailing mat of small rounded leaves across the forest floor, but its paired summer flowers are distinctly pink-flushed rather than pure white, deepening in color toward the lobe tips. It spreads by rooting at the nodes as it creeps, making it a slow but reliable groundcover for a shaded rock garden, terrarium, or woodland container where a North American gardener wants to compare it directly against native Mitchella repens. Give it the same cool, consistently moist, acidic humus favored by its American relative, and avoid any lime or alkaline amendment. It is offered only by a handful of specialty woodland and alpine nurseries, so source nursery-propagated divisions rather than expecting typical garden-center availability.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this patented sport is the only widely sold variegated wintergreen and stays notably smaller and slower than the plain-leaved species.

directions: Winter Splash is a US-patented sport of eastern teaberry selected for leaves splashed in white and green that blush pink across the whole leaf surface once cold weather arrives, turning the dwarf mound into a two-toned winter accent rather than the uniform dark green of the wild species. White, nodding, urn-shaped summer flowers give way to the same bright scarlet, wintergreen-scented berries typical of the species, which stand out vividly against the pale variegated foliage. It stays notably more compact and slower-spreading than straight-species Gaultheria procumbens, making it a better fit for a small shaded rock garden pocket, container, or path edge than for covering large areas. Grow it exactly as other wintergreen selections, in cool, moist, acidic, humus-rich soil beneath established trees or ericaceous shrubs, and avoid any lime-amended or poorly drained site.
sources: Broken Arrow Nursery — Gaultheria procumbens 'Gaulbri1' plant profile
Briggs Nursery — Winter Splash cultivar notes

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this UK-raised selection forms a dense, compact mound and takes five to ten years to reach its full mature spread.

directions: Big Berry is a compact, mound-forming wintergreen selection bred for an unusually heavy and oversized crop of glossy dark red fruit, carried on glossy, oval evergreen leaves that flush red, purple, and bronze through the cold months. Racemes of small white to pale pink, bell-shaped flowers open in summer and are followed by the outsized berries that give the cultivar its name, persisting on the plant well into winter. Its dense, slow, tidy habit fills in over several years to form a weed-suppressing evergreen carpet under acid-loving shrubs or at the edge of a shaded rock garden, without the looser, more open look of the wild species. Site it in the same cool, moist, acidic, humus-rich soil favored by other Gaultheria procumbens forms, sheltered from drying wind and winter sun.
sources: RHS Plant Finder — Gaultheria procumbens 'Big Berry' (Gaubi)
Shoot Gardening — Gaultheria procumbens 'Big Berry' plant guide

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or spring into well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; this species handles drier shade and leaner soil than the showier cultivated selections of its own kind already grown for patterned foliage.

directions: Little Heartleaf is the straight wild species behind the ornamentally patterned 'Dixie Darling' selection already grown in gardens, a narrow Piedmont and coastal-plain endemic found from Virginia south through the Carolinas into north-central South Carolina. Its small, leathery, heart-shaped evergreen leaves form a low, tight clump that spreads slowly by rhizome, holding attractive winter foliage with only modest silver mottling compared to its more dramatically patterned relatives. The jug-shaped, brownish flowers hide at ground level beneath the leaves in spring and are easy to overlook without parting the foliage. It tolerates drier, leaner soil than many other wild gingers once established, making it a useful choice for naturalizing beneath oaks or pines in a Piedmont woodland garden.
sources: North Carolina Native Plant Society — Wild Gingers (Hexastylis and Asarum) in North Carolina
Mt. Cuba Center — Little Heartleaf plant profile

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated divisions in fall or spring into moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade, recreating the bluff-base seeps and narrow ravine edges of its native habitat; never collect from wild populations.

directions: Dwarf-Flowered Heartleaf is the diminutive straight species behind the ornamental 'Eco Decor' selection already in cultivation, a rare North Carolina and South Carolina Piedmont endemic historically confined to narrow ravines and the moist bases of bluffs above streams and bogs. It forms a miniature, slowly spreading mat of small, dark, glossy, heart-shaped evergreen leaves rarely more than a few inches tall, with tiny yellowish flowers hidden at ground level in spring that are smaller than those of almost any other Asarum. Once listed as federally threatened, surveys have since found many more populations and it was removed from the federal list, though it remains a conservation-priority plant best grown from nursery-propagated stock rather than wild collection. In the garden it wants the same steady moisture, acidic humus, and dappled shade as its native seep-forest habitat, making it a specialty choice for a shaded streamside bed rather than a general-purpose groundcover.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service — Dwarf-Flowered Heartleaf species status
Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center — Hexastylis naniflora

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in fall or spring into moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade along a shaded stream bank or bog edge, mimicking the wet forest habitat of its small central Alabama range.

directions: Alabama Heartleaf is the wild straight species behind the 'Bloodshot Eyes' selection already represented in this dataset, a species of conservation concern found only in a small cluster of counties in central Alabama north of Montgomery. It carries triangular, silver-overlaid evergreen leaves with a mild anise scent when bruised, and in April and May produces the genus's characteristically wide, flat, owl-faced flowers in tan, purple, and maroon tones at ground level, larger and more open-faced than the flowers of most other wild gingers. In the wild it grows along shaded streams and seasonally wet bog edges, so garden plantings do best with consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil rather than the drier shade tolerated by some other southeastern Asarum species. Because its native range is so limited, plant only nursery-propagated divisions and treat it as a specialty addition to a shaded streamside or bog-edge woodland garden.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society — Asarum speciosum species profile
Flora of North America — Hexastylis speciosa
